approach: The time goes on the prosecutor reading counts twice, SJ's long Van Buren speech, Marcus's courtroom detour and a second round of questions after the peer-feedback reveal. The cut keeps the shape (counts and 151 years, the 09:14 timestamp SJ swallows, SJ shut down by the judge, Marcus betrayed by his own feedback, Brendan silent, 'the fourteenth') and drops the repeated or explanatory lines around each beat.

suggestions.title: Cut the prosecutor's last matter and Marcus's reply
suggestions.why: The peer-feedback quote is the scene's real blow to Marcus; the AWS-logs question repeats what s23_l10 and s23_l11 already established, and Marcus's 'Chinese AI did the hacking' restates his s22 position.
suggestions.keeps: The Chinese-model warning payoff stays in s22 and the quote in s23_l33. 'Thank you. No further questions' (s23_l41) follows straight on from Marcus's 'we were told nobody would see the raw feedback'.

against.s23_l39: One last matter. SJ's name showed up in the AWS logs on the night in question, is that correct?
against.s23_l40: .....yeah, but didn't cause the fucking world to end. Sure, he should have listened to me about not using the Chinese AI, but really, it was all the Chinese AI that did the hacking, not -.

suggestions.riskWhy: The AWS-logs question repeats s23_l10 and s23_l11, but Marcus's sweary half-defence is his last word in the trial and the only time he sticks up for SJ after the quote betrays him. No plot fact is lost: the Chinese-model warning is already in s22_backdoor and s22_unlocked.
loses: Character: Marcus defending SJ ('didn't cause the fucking world to end') right after his feedback is read out, then blaming the Chinese AI with an I-told-you-so
Joke: Marcus still making his Chinese-model point under oath, echoing s11b_l19 and s22_backdoor
Plot: SJ's name in the AWS logs, already stated in s23_l10, s23_l11 and s20_l66

suggestions.title: Read the counts once
suggestions.why: The second block of counts is the same joke as the first. The stage direction (s23_l4) already shows all nineteen rows entering on screen.
suggestions.keeps: Count one to four in s23_l3, the nineteen on screen, and Brendan's 151 years in s23_l8, which pays off in s23b and s23b.

against.s23_l5: counts eleven through fourteen, unauthorised access to a protected computer in furtherance of fraud. Counts fifteen and sixteen, damage to a protected computer. Count seventeen, aggravated identity theft.

suggestions.riskWhy: Pure repetition: the second block of counts is the same list joke as s23_l3, and s23_l4 already puts all nineteen on screen.
loses: Colour: the specific later charges (fraud, damage, aggravated identity theft) that make the pile-up sound absurd
Joke: the second round of the endless-counts gag, which plays as the topper to s23_l3

suggestions.title: Shorten SJ's Van Buren speech

edits.text: It's, it'll take nine seconds. It says "without authorisation." My access was never revoked. Nobody revoked it. There's a case, Van Buren, it's a Supreme Court case, and it's about exactly this. They gave it to me and they never took it back. That's not a crime, that's their filing system.

suggestions.why: The eleven-thousand-lines point about the model summary is a second argument that dilutes the first, and the case explanation restates 'never revoked'. The nine-seconds joke still lands because he overruns.
suggestions.keeps: SJ's pedantry and the never-revoked argument, which s23_l19 and s23b ('without authorisation') both depend on.

against.s23_l15: It's, it'll take nine seconds. It says "without authorisation." My access was never revoked. Nobody revoked it. There's a case, Van Buren, it's a Supreme Court case, and it's about exactly this, it's not about what you did with the access, it's about whether you had it. And I had it. They gave it to me and they never took it back. That's not a crime, that's their filing system. And nobody read eleven thousand lines. A model read them and wrote you a summary. It says what the tool said it ran. Not what it ran.

suggestions.riskWhy: Keeps the never-revoked argument that s24_l10 and the jury reaction depend on, but cuts SJ's second point, which is his own rule from s01c_l23 ('read your diffs, not the machine's summary') turned on the court. It also trims the clause that explains what Van Buren actually says.
loses: Character: SJ applying his s01c_l23 rule ('not the machine's summary') to the prosecution's evidence, a callback nowhere else in s23
Plot: the claim that the log summary was written by a model and records what the tool said it ran, not what it ran (echoes s20_l57 and s20_l66, stated nowhere else in the trial)
Joke: some of the overrun on 'it'll take nine seconds', which shrinks from about 39 to about 20 seconds

suggestions.title: Drop Brendan's 1986 law opener
suggestions.why: A history aside that nothing later refers to. The scene can open on the prosecutor reading count one.
suggestions.keeps: Brendan's commentary role starts at s23_l8 with the 151 years.

against.s23_l2: The law they used is from 1986. It was written after a film came out about a teenager starting a nuclear war with a modem...

suggestions.riskWhy: Nothing later refers to it, so no plot or setup is lost, but the modem-and-nuclear-war line is a unique laugh and the scene's only comment on how old and arbitrary the law is. Raised from low because it removes a distinct joke.
loses: Joke: the 1986 law written after a film about a teenager starting a nuclear war with a modem (nowhere else)
Colour: Brendan establishing his gallery-commentator role before the counts begin

suggestions.title: Cut Brendan's 'same act' commentary
suggestions.why: Two lines explaining the stacked counts before s23_l8 explains them again with the number that matters.
suggestions.keeps: The 151 years and the plea logic in s23_l8, and 'He wouldn't agree to it' (s23_l9).

against.s23_l6: Most of them are the same act, counted differently.
against.s23_l7: All nineteen of them are things that happened before four o'clock in the morning on one night in September.

suggestions.riskWhy: Mostly explanation that s23_l8 makes again with the number that matters. The one unique fact, that it all happened on one night in September before four in the morning, is not used anywhere else.
loses: Colour: 'one night in September', the only time the play dates the hack (nowhere else)
Character: Brendan's quiet 'same act, counted differently' irritation on SJ's behalf

suggestions.title: One Marcus Luddite line, then the judge
suggestions.why: Marcus gets cut off twice. Once is enough; the judge's full rebuke in s23_l27 does the work.
suggestions.keeps: The loom gag in s23_l24 (one instance per Marcus scene), the judge's 'Not to lecture us', and SJ's hand over his eyes.

against.s23_l26: I'm just trying to explain, because it's the same system, and an individual can do something that on the surface appears..

suggestions.riskWhy: The judge interrupting Marcus once still lands the reversal, and 'it's the same system' is repeated in s23b_l19 and s24_l36. Some rhythm is lost: two cut-offs build the gag better than one.
loses: Joke: the judge's double 'Mr. Ehrlich', which builds the turn-the-tables interruption
Character: Marcus's 'it's the same system' attempt, said again in s23b_l19

suggestions.title: Cut the gallery quip about Marcus
suggestions.why: A gallery aside that explains the joke the audience just watched. The judge cutting Marcus off and SJ's hand over his eyes already land it.
suggestions.keeps: Marcus being interrupted for once still plays on stage. Loses Kristina's only line in the scene.

against.s23_l29: You know, we really didn't give Marcus enough credit...
against.s23_l30: It's kind of fun to watch him interrupt someone else for a change

suggestions.riskWhy: Removes Kristina's only line in the trial and the gallery's payoff of the running gag where Marcus talks over her (s01_l28, s06_l9). That comedy is a guardrail, but its main instances in s01, s06 and s11b stay, so this cuts an echo, not the guardrail itself.
loses: Joke: Kristina enjoying Marcus being interrupted for once, paying off the talking-over-Kristina runner from s01 and s06
Joke: Brendan's deadpan 'we really didn't give Marcus enough credit'
Character: Kristina's only presence in s23; she becomes a silent figure in the gallery

suggestions.title: Trim the prosecutor's evidence line

edits.text: The device was recovered from the defendant's home. Every action in the log was taken as the defendant.

suggestions.why: 'The credentials used were issued to the defendant' repeats 'taken as the defendant' and the 01:58 line that follows. Leave s23_l11 whole: the 09:14 timestamp is what SJ reacts to.
suggestions.keeps: The machine found at SJ's (also in s22_l72), and the 09:14 beat in s23_l12 that sets up SJ shielding Brendan in s23b.

against.s23_l10: The device was recovered from the defendant's home. The credentials used were issued to the defendant. Every action in the log was taken as the defendant.

suggestions.riskWhy: Pure repetition: 'the credentials used were issued to the defendant' restates 'taken as the defendant' and the 01:58 line, and the same point is made in s20_l66 and s22_mine.
loses: Nothing substantive: the issued-credentials clause repeats s23_l10's last sentence and s23_l11

suggestions.title: Shorten the Marcus opener and the judge's warning

edits.text: Before I answer that, I want it noted that it took the British parliament eleven months. To make breaking a machine a hanging offence.
The log says what it says. Mr Mkrtchyan, I strongly advice you to remain silent.

suggestions.why: Marcus's 'never once moved that fast for a person' tail and the judge's 'let your attorney do the talking' both restate their first clause.
suggestions.keeps: 'I want it noted', the hanging offence (echoed by 'hanging' in s23b_l17), and the judge shutting SJ down.

against.s23_l24: Before I answer that, I want it noted that it took the British parliament eleven months. To make breaking a machine a hanging offence. Eleven months, start to finish, and they have never once moved that fast for a person, not in two hundred...
against.s23_l17: The log says what it says. Mr Mkrtchyan, I strongly advice you to remain silent and let your attorney do the talking.

suggestions.riskWhy: Both tails restate their first clause, and Marcus's point that the system protects machines over people is made again in s23b_l19 and s24_l36. If taken without #139, s23_l25's 'Mr. Ehrlich' interrupts a finished sentence, so the trailing '...' cut-off needs restaging; the edit also has a typo, 'advice' for 'advise'.
loses: Character: Marcus's conclusion that parliament 'never once moved that fast for a person', the point of his Luddite fact
Staging: Marcus being cut off mid-sentence ('not in two hundred...'), unless the actor trails off another way
Nothing substantive: 'let your attorney do the talking' restates 'remain silent'

suggestions.title: Trim Brendan's question in the gallery

edits.text: Do you think he's actually gonna get blamed for everything?

suggestions.why: 'I didn't think SJ was gonna get in trouble over this stuff' is implied by the question. The stage directions s23_l44 and s23_l45 (what SJ knows and feels) cannot read from the back row and could go at the same time, since s23_l43 and s23_l46 already stage both men not looking.
suggestions.keeps: Brendan's guilt beat and the frozen stillness of both men. SJ's reasoning is given aloud by the s23b narrator.

against.s23_l47: I didn't think SJ was gonna get in trouble over this stuff... Do you think he's actually gonna get blamed for everything?

suggestions.riskWhy: The question carries the guilt beat on its own. Note the keeps claim that an s23b narrator voices SJ's reasoning: s23b has no narrator, so if s23_l44 and s23_l45 also go, nothing spoken says SJ knows Brendan was at the machine at 09:14 beyond s23_l12.
loses: Character: Brendan admitting he never thought SJ would get in trouble, his naivety stated outright

suggestions.title: Cut 'He wasn't called by the defence'
suggestions.why: The prosecutor calling Marcus already shows which side called him.

against.s23_l22: He wasn't called by the defence.

suggestions.riskWhy: Not plot, but it is a dry laugh and the only signal before the testimony that Marcus is a hostile witness, which primes the peer-feedback betrayal in s23_l33. Raised from low because many audiences will not read 'the people call' as meaning the prosecution.
loses: Joke: Brendan's deadpan 'He wasn't called by the defence'
Setup: tells the audience Marcus is there against SJ before s23_l33 reveals why

suggestions.keeps: The praise that the peer-feedback quote then contradicts.

against.s23_l32: SJ? SJ's the best engineer I've ever worked with. He's difficult, obviously. Everyone knows that. But he's not... no, he's the best.

ifDeleted.summary: The Trial is the play's only courtroom: it states the nineteen counts and the 151-year maximum, lets SJ hear the 09:14 timestamp and realise Brendan was at the keyboard, pays off Marcus's anonymous peer feedback in open court, and shows Brendan choosing to stay silent in the gallery. s23b already carries SJ's reasoning for taking the fall, so the plot survives with a narrator bridge and two small trims, but Brendan's silent choice and the peer-feedback payoff go.

changes.detail: Narrator bridge carrying the trial, the 151 years, the 09:14 timestamp and Brendan's silence.
changes.text: NARRATOR: The trial takes three weeks. Nineteen counts. Add them up and it is a hundred and fifty-one years. The log says SJ started it at one fifty-eight and tidied up at nine fourteen. SJ knows who was at the keyboard at nine fourteen. He says nothing. Brendan sits three rows back every day, and says nothing either.

changes.detail: Setup for the peer-feedback reveal that no longer happens.

ifDeleted.riskWhy: The plot survives through s23b, but the play loses its only public reckoning and Brendan's on-stage choice to let SJ take the blame, which a narrator line can report but cannot play.
